nodes.label: Neo-Assyrian Empire
nodes.full: The dominant power of the age: Sargon II's conquest of Babylonia brought the Assyrian frontier to the head of the Gulf, and the kings of Dilmun judged it prudent to send gifts, tribute and labour.
nodes.src: background — Fuchs (1994); Frame (1992).

nodes.label: Babylon
nodes.full: The old imperial city Dilmun had once been a province of: sacked by Sennacherib, rebuilt with Dilmun bronze and labour, and after 626 BC the seat of the Neo-Babylonian kings who replaced Assyria.
nodes.src: background — Beaulieu, 'A History of Babylon' (2018).

nodes.label: Gerrha and the mainland tribes
nodes.full: The Aramaic- and Arabic-speaking tribal world spreading across eastern Arabia, and the new caravan city of Gerrha rising from it to draw the Gulf trade to the mainland.
nodes.src: background — Eph'al, 'The Ancient Arabs' (1982); Potts (1990) vol.2.

nodes.label: The Chaldeans of the marshes
nodes.full: Merodach-baladan's Bit-Yakin Chaldeans at the head of the Gulf — the nearer, more dangerous neighbour against whom Dilmun chose to side with distant Assyria.
nodes.src: background — Frame, 'Babylonia 689–627 BC' (1992).

nodes.label: Uperi, king of Dilmun, submits to Sargon II of Assyria
nodes.full: Sargon II records that Uperi, king of Dilmun, 'whose abode is situated at a distance of 30 double-hours in the midst of the sea of the rising sun', heard of his power and sent gifts. It is the first time a Dilmun king is named in a foreign record.
nodes.src: Sargon II, Annals and Display Inscription (Khorsabad), 709 BC (Fuchs, 'Die Inschriften Sargons II.', 1994).

nodes.label: Hundaru of Dilmun pays tribute to Sennacherib and Ashurbanipal
nodes.full: Hundaru, king of Dilmun, sends tribute — bronze, dates, precious woods — to Sennacherib and again to Ashurbanipal, and provides labourers and bronze for the rebuilding of Babylon. Dilmun survives as a small tributary kingdom on the Assyrian world's edge.
nodes.src: Sennacherib inscriptions (Chicago Prism) and Ashurbanipal's records; Hundaru's tribute and corvée for Babylon noted in Frame, 'Babylonia 689–627 BC' (1992).

nodes.label: Dilmun aids Assyria against the Chaldeans
nodes.full: When Sennacherib campaigned against Merodach-baladan's Chaldeans in the southern marshes, Dilmun sent troops and workmen to help — aligning with distant Assyria against a nearer, more dangerous neighbour on the Gulf head.
nodes.src: Sennacherib's sixth campaign account; Dilmun's assistance in Frame, 'Babylonia 689–627 BC' (1992), ch. 3.

nodes.label: Nomad and Chaldean raiding on the Dilmun mainland
nodes.full: As Aramaean and Chaldean tribes spread down the western Gulf, the mainland Dilmun districts around Qatif and Tarut became exposed to raiding. The island core on Bahrain was defensible; the coast was not.
nodes.src: Inferential from the pattern of Neo-Assyrian references to Aramaean/Chaldean tribes reaching the Gulf; Potts, 'The Arabian Gulf in Antiquity' vol. 1 (1990), ch. 8.

nodes.label: Rise of Gerrha and the shift of Gulf power to the mainland
nodes.full: By the end of Dilmun's span a new mainland trading power, Gerrha, was emerging in eastern Arabia, drawing the caravan and sea trade to itself. Dilmun's centuries as the Gulf's indispensable middleman were ending.
nodes.src: Gerrha first clearly attested by later Classical authors (Strabo, Pliny) but its rise is placed in the earlier 1st millennium BC; Potts (1990) vol. 2, ch. 2.

nodes.label: The kingship of Dilmun revived
nodes.full: After the Kassite governorship lapsed with the fall of Kassite Babylon, Dilmun re-emerges in the record with kings of its own — Uperi, then Hundaru — who could raise tribute, levy labourers and send envoys. A province had become a small independent monarchy again.
nodes.src: Inferred from the Neo-Assyrian royal inscriptions naming Dilmun kings (Fuchs 1994; Frame, 'Babylonia 689–627 BC', 1992); the intervening gap discussed in Potts (1990) vol. 1, ch. 8.

nodes.label: The Late Dilmun palace at Qal'at al-Bahrain
nodes.full: A substantial columned building of the City IV horizon at Qal'at al-Bahrain — the so-called Late Dilmun palace — with storerooms, snake-bowl foundation deposits and imported goods, marks the island's administrative centre in the Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian centuries.
nodes.src: French mission at Qal'at al-Bahrain (Lombard & Kervran); the City IV 'palace' published in Lombard (ed.), 'Bahrain: la civilisation des deux mers' (1999).

nodes.label: Inzak endures in the first-millennium record
nodes.full: The Dilmun god Inzak, 'lord of Agarum', is still slotted into Mesopotamian god-lists copied in the first millennium, and a Sealand-era royal name had already been compounded with his. The old religion of Dilmun outlived the Bronze Age trade that spread its name.
nodes.src: Inzak in the god-list An = Anum and its first-millennium copies; Kh. Nashef, 'The Deities of Dilmun' (1986); the Sealand king Ea-gamil / Inzak-names in Potts (1990) vol. 1.

nodes.label: Snake-bowl deposits at the Late Dilmun palace
nodes.full: Bowls holding the bones of sea snakes, sometimes with a bead, were laid in the foundations of the City IV building at Qal'at al-Bahrain — the same rite recorded in the Bronze-Age town centuries earlier. Ritual practice on the island ran in a continuous thread.
nodes.src: The City IV snake-bowl deposits (Lombard, 'Bahrain: la civilisation des deux mers', 1999); the Bronze-Age antecedents in Bibby, 'Looking for Dilmun' (1969).

nodes.label: Imported goods in the Late Dilmun assemblage
nodes.full: The Late Dilmun material record — glazed vessels, Assyrian-style bronzes, glass and beads in the City IV building and the late graves — shows an island still plugged into the northern luxury network, but now as a recipient of Mesopotamian and Assyrian fashion rather than a maker of its own brand.
nodes.src: Late Dilmun finds from Qal'at al-Bahrain City IV and the Shakhoura / al-Maqsha cemeteries (Lombard 1999); the disappearance of the distinctive Barbar red ridged ware after the Bronze Age (Højlund, Failaka vol. 2, 1987).

nodes.label: 'Thirty double-hours in the midst of the sea'
nodes.full: Sargon II's scribes recorded Dilmun as lying 'at a distance of 30 double-hours in the midst of the sea of the rising sun' — a measured, if schematic, statement of where the island was. Even a diminished Dilmun kept a precise place in Mesopotamian geographical knowledge.
nodes.src: Sargon II, Display Inscription and Annals (Fuchs, 'Die Inschriften Sargons II. aus Khorsabad', 1994); Horowitz, 'Mesopotamian Cosmic Geography' (1998).

nodes.label: Dilmun pearls — the 'fish-eyes' of cuneiform
nodes.full: An Assyrian text lists 'fish-eyes' from Dilmun among tribute goods — almost certainly pearls from the banks off Bahrain. The fishery that began in the Neolithic was now feeding a luxury market in the Mesopotamian and Assyrian courts.
nodes.src: Neo-Assyrian reference to 'eyes of fish' from Dilmun (discussed by Potts 1990); the identification with pearls is standard though not certain.

nodes.label: The tribute economy — bronze, dates and woods
nodes.full: The goods Uperi and Hundaru sent north — bronze, dates, precious timbers, and the pearls the Assyrians called 'fish-eyes' — are a list of what Late Dilmun still produced or could obtain. The island had lost the transit trade but kept its gardens, its smiths and its pearl banks.
nodes.src: Sennacherib and Ashurbanipal inscriptions on Dilmun's tribute and corvée for Babylon; Frame, 'Babylonia 689–627 BC' (1992), ch. 3.

nodes.label: The Gulf sea route still worked
nodes.full: Dilmun's envoys and its tribute reached Nineveh and Babylon by the same sea road up the Gulf that the Bronze-Age copper ships had used. The sewn-plank, bitumen-caulked boat and the seasonal sailing pattern outlasted the trade that had built them.
nodes.src: Continuity of Gulf watercraft argued from bitumen boat fragments across periods (Carter 2006); the logistics of Dilmun's Assyrian-era contacts in Potts (1990) vol. 1.

nodes.label: Iron reaches the Gulf
nodes.full: The first millennium BC brought iron tools and weapons into eastern Arabia alongside the older bronze, part of the same technological shift transforming the wider Near East. It reached Dilmun as an import, worked up by the island's long-established metalworkers.
nodes.src: The Iron Age transition in south-east Arabia (Magee, 'The Archaeology of Prehistoric Arabia', 2014); iron finds in Late Dilmun contexts noted by Lombard (1999).

nodes.label: Dilmun envoys at the Assyrian court
nodes.full: The gifts Uperi and Hundaru sent to Sargon II, Sennacherib and Ashurbanipal were carried by envoys making the long journey up the Gulf and overland. Even reduced, Dilmun maintained formal relations with the dominant power of the age.
nodes.src: Sargon II and Sennacherib royal inscriptions; Frame, 'Babylonia 689–627 BC' (1992).

nodes.label: Dilmun labour and bronze for the rebuilding of Babylon
nodes.full: Esarhaddon's and Ashurbanipal's records credit the king of Dilmun with sending workmen and bronze for the reconstruction of Babylon after Sennacherib's sack. A small Gulf kingdom was contributing, on demand, to the imperial building programme of the age.
nodes.src: Neo-Assyrian building inscriptions on the restoration of Babylon; Dilmun's contribution in Frame, 'Babylonia 689–627 BC' (1992).

nodes.label: The mainland fills with new Arab tribes
nodes.full: As Aramaic- and early Arabic-speaking tribes spread across eastern Arabia and the domesticated camel opened the interior, the old Dilmun mainland around Qatif and Tarut passed into a new tribal world — the one from which Gerrha would rise and, centuries later, the Arab Gulf.
nodes.src: Eph'al, 'The Ancient Arabs' (1982); the camel and the north-Arabian trade in Macdonald's studies of ancient Arabia; Potts (1990) vol. 2 on Gerrha's background.

nodes.label: Neo-Assyrian power reaches the Gulf
nodes.full: Sargon II's conquest of Babylonia brought the Assyrian frontier to the marshes at the head of the Gulf, close enough that the kings of Dilmun judged it prudent to send tribute. Dilmun's last documented century is spent in Assyria's orbit.
nodes.src: Sargon II, Sennacherib and Ashurbanipal inscriptions; Frame (1992).

nodes.label: Aramaeans and Chaldeans spread down the western Gulf
nodes.full: The first millennium BC brought new Semitic-speaking tribal populations — Aramaeans, then Chaldeans — into the lands between Mesopotamia and Dilmun. Their arrival reshaped the political map of the Gulf that Dilmun had long dominated.
nodes.src: Neo-Assyrian references to Aramaean and Chaldean tribes; Eph'al, 'The Ancient Arabs' (1982).

nodes.label: Assyria falls, Babylon rises
nodes.full: Within a generation of Ashurbanipal's death the Assyrian empire collapsed and the Neo-Babylonian kings took its place. Dilmun's last century of documentation ends as the northern power to which it answered was destroyed — and the record of the island goes quiet until the Persian and Greek age.
nodes.src: The fall of Nineveh (612 BC) and the Neo-Babylonian succession (standard chronology; Beaulieu, 'A History of Babylon', 2018); the gap in Dilmun's documentation in Potts (1990) vol. 2, ch. 1.

nodes.label: From mounds to cist graves
nodes.full: The great Bronze-Age mound cemeteries were no longer being extended. First-millennium Dilmun buried its dead in simpler stone cist graves, sometimes cut into or beside the old mounds — a quieter mortuary landscape for a quieter island.
nodes.src: Late Dilmun burials at Shakhoura and al-Maqsha (Lombard 1999); the end of primary mound construction after the Bronze Age (S.F. Andersen, Bahrain Burial Mounds project).

nodes.label: A diminished population on the island
nodes.full: The settlement record — a contracted town at Qal'at al-Bahrain, fewer sites, smaller cemeteries — points to a Late Dilmun population well below the Bronze-Age peak. The island endured as a working kingdom, but a small one, sustained by its springs and its pearl banks.
nodes.src: Settlement contraction across the City III–IV horizons (Højlund & Andersen, 'Qala'at al-Bahrain'; Lombard 1999); the general first-millennium picture in Potts (1990) vol. 1.
